An orphan keeps running under a new parent, and PID 1 always waits for its children, so an orphan never stays a zombie for long. The problem case is a live parent that never calls wait() — then its dead children pile up as zombies. In a container, PID 1 must do this reaping.
man 2 wait; man 2 prctl (PR_SET_CHILD_SUBREAPER)

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What does fork() followed by exec() do?
passages.text:
What does fork() followed by exec() do?
This is how a shell starts every command: the child inherits open file descriptors (which is how redirections work) and environment, then execve loads the new binary into it while the PID stays the same. Threads come from clone with shared memory.
man 2 fork; man 2 execve

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What is the main difference between a thread and a process o
passages.text:
What is the main difference between a thread and a process on Linux?
Both are tasks created with clone(); threads pass flags that share memory, file table and signal handlers. Threads can run in parallel on several CPUs, and ps -L or top -H shows them individually.
man 2 clone; man 7 pthreads

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: Why does Python's GIL keep CPU-bound threads from speeding u
passages.text:
Why does Python's GIL keep CPU-bound threads from speeding up, while I/O-bound threads still help?
In CPython with the GIL, threads take turns running bytecode, so pure computation is not parallel; blocking calls such as socket reads release it so other threads can progress. For CPU work, use multiprocessing, or a free-threaded build of Python 3.13 or later.
https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-global-interpreter-lock; https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What does `ulimit -n` control?
passages.text:
What does `ulimit -n` control?
A server that fails with "Too many open files" has hit RLIMIT_NOFILE, and sockets count. For a systemd service the limit comes from LimitNOFILE= in the unit, not from the shell or /etc/security/limits.conf. Processes are -u and file size is -f.
man 1 bash (ulimit); man 2 getrlimit; man 5 systemd.exec (LimitNOFILE)

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: A process's memory usage grows steadily over days until the
passages.text:
A process's memory usage grows steadily over days until the OOM killer ends it. What does that most suggest?
Steady growth of RSS under a steady workload is the signature of a leak — in garbage-collected languages, often an ever-growing cache or list. Page cache is reclaimed on demand and not charged to the process like this; disabling swap changes when OOM happens, not why.
man 5 proc (/proc/pid/status, VmRSS)

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What does "overcommit" mean in Linux memory management?
passages.text:
What does "overcommit" mean in Linux memory management?
malloc usually succeeds because pages are only backed when first written. If too many are touched, the OOM killer reclaims memory by killing a process. vm.overcommit_memory selects the heuristic (0), always (1) or strict accounting (2).
https://docs.kernel.org/mm/overcommit-accounting.html

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What is a page?
passages.text:
What is a page?
Virtual addresses are translated page by page through page tables, and the TLB caches recent translations. Some ARM64 systems use 16 KiB pages, and huge pages (2 MiB, 1 GiB) reduce TLB misses for large memory users. getconf PAGESIZE prints the base size.
https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/concepts.html

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
A Python str counts code points, but UTF-8 encodes é in two bytes. Byte lengths matter wherever a limit is in bytes — a database column, a protocol header, a file name on disk.
https://docs.python.org/3/howto/unicode.html

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
In two's complement, -1 has every bit set, so masking with 0xFF keeps eight ones: 255. XOR of 1010 and 0110 is 1100, which is 12. Shifting 1 left by 10 bits multiplies by 2^10.
https://docs.python.org/3/reference/expressions.html#binary-bitwise-operations

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
Octal 755 is 7·64 + 5·8 + 5 = 493, which is why file modes are written in octal: each digit is three permission bits. oct and hex return strings with the 0o and 0x prefixes, lower-case.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#int

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 have no exact binary representation, and the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare floats with a tolerance (math.isclose), and keep money in integers or Decimal.
https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/floatingpoint.html

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What is the time complexity of checking `x in s` for a Pytho
passages.text:
What is the time complexity of checking `x in s` for a Python set, and for a list, of n elements?
A set is a hash table: hashing the element leads almost directly to its slot. A list has to be scanned element by element. Turning a list of allowed hosts into a set before a loop that checks thousands of lines is a common, large speed-up.
https://wiki.python.org/moin/TimeComplexity

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: Why is reading a file sequentially usually much faster than
passages.text:
Why is reading a file sequentially usually much faster than reading the same bytes at random offsets on a hard disk?
A seek costs milliseconds on a spinning disk, and the kernel detects sequential access and reads ahead into the page cache. SSDs remove the seek, so the gap shrinks but read-ahead still helps. iostat -x shows the resulting await times.
man 1 iostat; https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/concepts.html

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What does `sync` do?
passages.text:
What does `sync` do?
Writes normally land in memory and are written out later, which is why pulling a USB stick without unmounting loses data. sync forces the write-out; fsync does it for one file from a program. Dropping caches is echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches, and rsync copies files.
man 1 sync; man 2 fsync

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: iowait is high in top, but the CPUs are otherwise idle. What
passages.text:
iowait is high in top, but the CPUs are otherwise idle. What does that indicate?
iowait is idle time during which some task was blocked on I/O; the bottleneck is storage, not CPU. iostat -x and iotop show which device and which process. A busy loop shows as us or sy, interrupts as hi and si.
man 1 top; man 1 iostat

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What does the `st` (steal) value in top mean on a virtual ma
passages.text:
What does the `st` (steal) value in top mean on a virtual machine?
High steal means the host is oversubscribed: the guest is ready to run but the physical CPU is busy elsewhere. Nothing inside the guest can fix it; a larger or dedicated instance can. sy is kernel time, and id is idle.
man 1 top

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: How does a cgroup memory limit, such as MemoryMax= on a syst
passages.text:
How does a cgroup memory limit, such as MemoryMax= on a systemd service or --memory on a container, behave when it is exceeded?
A cgroup is its own memory domain: page cache charged to it is reclaimed first, and if that is not enough the OOM killer acts inside the group, leaving the rest of the system alone. MemoryHigh= throttles by reclaiming harder before that point.
https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html#memory; man 5 systemd.resource-control

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What does `strace -f -e trace=openat ./app` show?
passages.text:
What does `strace -f -e trace=openat ./app` show?
strace intercepts system calls; -f follows forked children and -e trace= filters the calls. A failing openat with ENOENT or EACCES is often the whole explanation for "it cannot find its config". ltrace traces library calls, and tcpdump captures packets.
man 1 strace

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What does `lsof -p 1234` list?
passages.text:
What does `lsof -p 1234` list?
Everything a process holds is a file descriptor in /proc/1234/fd, and lsof names each one: regular files, deleted files still open, TCP and UDP sockets, pipes. Threads are in /proc/1234/task.
man 8 lsof; man 5 proc

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: Why can a program's stdout appear in a different order relat
passages.text:
Why can a program's stdout appear in a different order relative to its stderr when both are redirected to one file?
The C library (and Python) line-buffers stdout on a terminal but buffers it in blocks when it goes to a file or pipe, so stdout text is written later, in chunks. stdbuf -oL, python -u or an explicit flush restores the interleaving.
man 3 setbuf; man 1 stdbuf

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
On a 64-bit build, sys.maxsize is the largest value a signed 64-bit index can hold. Python integers are arbitrary precision, so 2**100 is a normal int and simply larger; there is no overflow as in C.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.maxsize

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What is a race condition?
passages.text:
What is a race condition?
Two scripts that read a counter, add one and write it back can both read 5 and both write 6. Locks (flock), atomic operations (rename, O_EXCL, INSERT … ON CONFLICT) and transactions remove the window. A deadlock is a different failure: each waits for the other forever.
man 1 flock; man 2 rename

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: Why do configuration tools write a new file and rename it ov
passages.text:
Why do configuration tools write a new file and rename it over the old one instead of editing in place?
A process or a crash during an in-place write can leave a truncated file. Writing to a temporary file in the same directory, fsyncing it and renaming it replaces the file in one step. The rename does give the path a new inode, which is also why an editor can break a hard link.
man 2 rename

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
SHA-256 produces 256 bits, which is 32 bytes, and each byte is two hexadecimal characters. The length never depends on the input, which is what lets a digest pin an image or a download.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/hashlib.html

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What does the kernel's page cache do when an application rea
passages.text:
What does the kernel's page cache do when an application reads the same file twice?
File contents read once stay in otherwise unused RAM until memory is needed elsewhere. That is why a second grep over a large log is much faster, why "buff/cache" is large on a healthy machine, and why benchmarks drop caches first.
https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/mm/concepts.html#page-cache

passages.title: Memory and CS in Linux: What does `vmstat 1` show in the si and so columns?
passages.text:
What does `vmstat 1` show in the si and so columns?
Sustained non-zero so means the machine is pushing memory to swap because RAM is short, and si that it is paying to bring it back — the pattern of a system that is thrashing. Swap merely being used, with si and so at zero, is harmless. Interrupts are the in column.
man 8 vmstat

passages.title: Networking: Which command shows listening TCP sockets together with the
passages.text:
Which command shows listening TCP sockets together with the owning process?
ss -t selects TCP, -l listening sockets, -n skips name resolution, -p shows the process. ip route and netstat -r print the routing table; ip neigh shows the neighbour (ARP) cache.
man 8 ss

passages.title: Networking: How many usable host addresses does 192.168.10.0/26 have?
passages.text:
How many usable host addresses does 192.168.10.0/26 have?
A /26 leaves 6 host bits: 2^6 = 64 addresses. The first is the network address and the last the broadcast address, which leaves 62 for hosts. 30 is a /27, 126 a /25.
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4632

passages.title: Networking: Which file decides whether host names are looked up in /etc/
passages.text:
Which file decides whether host names are looked up in /etc/hosts or DNS first?
The hosts line in nsswitch.conf (for example "hosts: files dns") sets the order of sources. resolv.conf lists the DNS servers to use once DNS is consulted; /etc/hostname is this machine's name; /etc/services maps service names to ports.
man 5 nsswitch.conf

passages.title: Networking: Which command shows the default route?
passages.text:
Which command shows the default route?
The routing table lives under ip route; "default" filters for the default route. ip addr shows addresses, ip link interfaces and their state, ip neigh the ARP/NDP cache.
man 8 ip-route

passages.title: Networking: Which ranges are private IPv4 address space as defined in RF
passages.text:
Which ranges are private IPv4 address space as defined in RFC 1918?
RFC 1918 reserves exactly three blocks: 10/8, 172.16/12 and 192.168/16. 100.64/10 is carrier-grade NAT space (RFC 6598) and 169.254/16 is link-local (RFC 3927) — both non-routable, neither RFC 1918.
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1918

passages.title: Networking: curl says "Connection refused" immediately. What is the most
passages.text:
curl says "Connection refused" immediately. What is the most likely cause?
Refused means the peer answered the SYN with a reset — typically because no socket listens there. A silent drop shows up as a timeout instead; a resolution failure is reported before any connection; a TLS problem happens after the TCP connection is established.
man 7 tcp; man 1 curl

passages.title: Networking: What does `firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8090/tcp` do
passages.text:
What does `firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8090/tcp` do on its own?
--permanent writes the zone's configuration without touching runtime. Follow it with firewall-cmd --reload, or run the same command without --permanent as well. Without --zone it applies to the default zone only.
man 1 firewall-cmd

passages.title: Networking: Which transport and port do ordinary DNS queries use?
passages.text:
Which transport and port do ordinary DNS queries use?
Plain DNS uses port 53, over UDP for ordinary queries and TCP for large answers and zone transfers. 853 is DNS over TLS, 123/udp is NTP and 25/tcp is SMTP.
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035

passages.title: Networking: After `nmcli connection modify eth0 +ipv4.addresses 10.1.1.5
passages.text:
After `nmcli connection modify eth0 +ipv4.addresses 10.1.1.5/24`, when does the interface get the address?
connection modify edits the stored profile. The change reaches the interface when the profile is (re)applied: nmcli connection up, nmcli device reapply, or the next boot. Additional static addresses also work alongside DHCP (method auto).
man 1 nmcli

passages.title: Networking: On Ethernet with a 1500-byte MTU, what is the largest TCP pa
passages.text:
On Ethernet with a 1500-byte MTU, what is the largest TCP payload per IPv4 segment without options?
The MTU covers the IP packet: 1500 minus a 20-byte IPv4 header minus a 20-byte TCP header leaves 1460, the usual MSS. 1480 subtracts only the IP header; 1472 is the ICMP/UDP payload (1500 − 20 − 8).
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9293

passages.title: Networking: Which IPv4 block is reserved for loopback?
passages.text:
Which IPv4 block is reserved for loopback?
The whole 127/8 block is loopback, though 127.0.0.1 is the address everyone uses. 0.0.0.0/8 means "this network", and 169.254/16 is link-local.
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5735

passages.title: Networking: What is the broadcast address of 172.16.5.130/25?
passages.text:
What is the broadcast address of 172.16.5.130/25?
A /25 splits the last octet into 0–127 and 128–255. .130 is in the upper half, whose network address is .128 and broadcast .255; the usable hosts are .129 to .254.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4632

passages.title: Networking: Which prefix length gives exactly 30 usable host addresses?
passages.text:
Which prefix length gives exactly 30 usable host addresses?
A /27 leaves 5 host bits: 2^5 = 32 addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses, is 30. A /28 has 14 usable hosts, a /26 62, and a /30 two — the classic point-to-point link.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4632

passages.title: Networking: Two hosts are 10.0.1.20/23 and 10.0.0.200/23. Can they reach
passages.text:
Two hosts are 10.0.1.20/23 and 10.0.0.200/23. Can they reach each other without a router?
A /23 spans two /24s: 10.0.0.0 to 10.0.1.255. Both addresses fall inside, so each host considers the other on-link and sends ARP for it directly. Looking only at the third octet is correct for /24 and nothing else.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4632

passages.title: Networking: Which command asks the kernel which route, source address an
passages.text:
Which command asks the kernel which route, source address and interface it would use to reach 1.1.1.1?
ip route get performs a real routing-table lookup and prints the chosen gateway, device and source address, including policy rules — without sending a packet. traceroute sends probes, ip neigh shows the ARP/NDP cache, and dig resolves names.
man 8 ip-route

passages.title: Networking: Which route does the kernel pick for a packet to 10.1.2.3 wh
passages.text:
Which route does the kernel pick for a packet to 10.1.2.3 when it has 10.0.0.0/8 via A, 10.1.0.0/16 via B and a default route via C?
IP routing uses the most specific match: /16 beats /8, and the default route (0.0.0.0/0) matches everything but is the least specific. Metrics only choose between routes of the same prefix length.
man 8 ip-route; https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1812#section-5.2.4.3

passages.title: Networking: Which command sends a DNS query to the server 9.9.9.9 direct
passages.text:
Which command sends a DNS query to the server 9.9.9.9 directly, bypassing /etc/resolv.conf?
dig @server asks that server and prints the full answer, flags and timing. getent uses the system's resolver order (nsswitch.conf, hosts file included), which is what applications see; host's -t selects a record type, not a server.
man 1 dig; man 1 getent

passages.title: Networking: `dig norboten.org` works, but `curl https://norboten.org` fa
passages.text:
`dig norboten.org` works, but `curl https://norboten.org` fails with "Could not resolve host". What is the likeliest difference?
dig bypasses the C library's resolver, so a broken hosts line in nsswitch.conf, a bad /etc/hosts entry or a failing local stub resolver only shows up for normal programs. getent hosts norboten.org reproduces what curl sees.
man 5 nsswitch.conf; man 1 getent

passages.title: Networking: Which DNS record type maps a name to an IPv6 address?
passages.text:
Which DNS record type maps a name to an IPv6 address?
A holds IPv4 addresses and AAAA IPv6. PTR maps an address back to a name (reverse DNS), and a CNAME makes one name an alias of another. A6 was an experimental IPv6 type, now historic.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3596

passages.title: Networking: Why can't a CNAME record exist at the apex of a zone, such a
passages.text:
Why can't a CNAME record exist at the apex of a zone, such as norboten.org itself?
RFC 1034 says a name with a CNAME has no other data, and a zone apex always has SOA and NS. Providers work around it with flattened "ALIAS" or "ANAME" records that resolve the target and serve plain A/AAAA answers.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1034#section-3.6.2

passages.title: Networking: A DNS record was changed ten minutes ago, but some clients s
passages.text:
A DNS record was changed ten minutes ago, but some clients still get the old address. What controls how long that lasts?
Resolvers may keep an answer for its TTL, so a record with a 3600-second TTL can be stale for up to an hour after a change. Lowering the TTL well before a migration shortens the window. The serial tells secondary servers to transfer the zone.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1035#section-3.2.1

passages.title: Networking: A connection attempt hangs for a long time and then times ou
passages.text:
A connection attempt hangs for a long time and then times out, instead of failing immediately. What does that usually mean?
A closed port answers with a TCP RST, which is an immediate "Connection refused". A timeout means the SYN got no answer at all: a DROP rule, a wrong route, or a host that is down. firewalld's default reject answers with ICMP and fails fast too.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9293

passages.title: Networking: A service listens on 127.0.0.1:8080. Why can't other machine
passages.text:
A service listens on 127.0.0.1:8080. Why can't other machines reach it even with the firewall open?
A socket bound to 127.0.0.1 accepts only traffic that arrives on the loopback interface. To accept remote connections, bind to the host's address or 0.0.0.0 (all IPv4 addresses) — ss -tlnp shows which address each socket is bound to.
man 8 ss; man 7 ip

passages.title: Networking: A web server shows thousands of sockets in TIME_WAIT. Which
passages.text:
A web server shows thousands of sockets in TIME_WAIT. Which statement is correct?
The endpoint that sends the first FIN waits about twice the maximum segment lifetime so that delayed packets of the old connection are not mistaken for a new one. It costs little memory and no process. A SYN flood shows up as SYN_RECV.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9293#section-3.6; man 8 ss

passages.title: Networking: Which is the TCP three-way handshake?
passages.text:
Which is the TCP three-way handshake?
The client sends SYN with its initial sequence number, the server answers SYN-ACK with its own, and the client acknowledges with ACK. FIN is for closing, and HELLO belongs to TLS, which runs on top of the established connection.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9293#section-3.5

passages.title: Networking: Which of these uses UDP?
passages.text:
Which of these uses UDP?
NTP runs on UDP port 123. SSH (22), HTTP/2 over TLS (443) and SMTP (25, 587) all run over TCP. HTTP/3 is the web protocol that moved to UDP, through QUIC.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5905

passages.title: Networking: Which command makes firewalld allow HTTPS now and after a re
passages.text:
Which command makes firewalld allow HTTPS now and after a reboot?
--permanent writes the configuration but does not touch the running rules, and a runtime-only change is lost at the next reload or boot. Either do both, reload after --permanent, or make the runtime change and then run firewall-cmd --runtime-to-permanent.
man 1 firewall-cmd

passages.title: Networking: A service runs on port 8090 on Rocky Linux. The firewall all
passages.text:
A service runs on port 8090 on Rocky Linux. The firewall allows it, yet nginx cannot connect to it as a reverse proxy and the audit log shows an AVC denial. What is the targeted fix?
SELinux stops httpd_t from opening outgoing network connections unless the boolean is on; -P keeps it across reboots. setenforce 0 disables enforcement for everything, file modes are not the problem, and the firewall does not govern local connections. (httpd_can_network_connect_db covers only database ports.)
man 8 setsebool; man 8 httpd_selinux

passages.title: Networking: sshd is moved to port 2222 on an SELinux-enforcing system an
passages.text:
sshd is moved to port 2222 on an SELinux-enforcing system and fails to bind. Which command fixes it?
SELinux labels ports, and sshd may bind only ports labelled ssh_port_t — 22 by default. semanage port -a adds 2222 to that type permanently. File contexts (chcon, restorecon) do not apply to ports, and there is no such boolean. Open the port in the firewall too.
man 8 semanage-port

passages.title: Networking: Which nmcli command gives the connection "eth0" a static add
passages.text:
Which nmcli command gives the connection "eth0" a static address and gateway?
A static profile needs method manual plus the addresses (and usually gateway and DNS). With method auto, DHCP is still used. nmcli dev set changes device properties, not addresses. Apply the change with nmcli con up eth0.
man 1 nmcli; man 5 nm-settings-nmcli

passages.title: Networking: Where does NetworkManager on Rocky Linux 10 store connection
passages.text:
Where does NetworkManager on Rocky Linux 10 store connection profiles?
RHEL 9 made the keyfile format the default, and RHEL 10 removed support for ifcfg files. /etc/network/interfaces belongs to Debian's ifupdown, and netplan to Ubuntu.
man 5 nm-settings-keyfile

passages.title: Networking: What does ARP do?
passages.text:
What does ARP do?
Before sending a frame to an on-link address or to the gateway, a host broadcasts an ARP request and caches the reply (ip neigh). IPv6 does the same with Neighbour Discovery. DHCP assigns addresses and DNS resolves names.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc826; man 8 ip-neighbour

passages.title: Networking: A host has the address 10.0.0.5/24 and the default gateway 1
passages.text:
A host has the address 10.0.0.5/24 and the default gateway 10.0.1.1. What happens?
A next hop must be reachable directly, and 10.0.1.1 is outside 10.0.0.0/24. ip route refuses to add it ("Nexthop has invalid gateway") unless forced with onlink, and even then nothing on the segment answers ARP for it unless the router really has that address there.
man 8 ip-route

passages.title: Networking: What does `curl -v https://example.com` show that helps sepa
passages.text:
What does `curl -v https://example.com` show that helps separate a TLS problem from an HTTP one?
-v prints lines starting with * for connection and TLS events, > for request headers and < for response headers. A failure before any > line is DNS, TCP or TLS; a 4xx or 5xx after them is the application.
man 1 curl

passages.title: Networking: Which command shows the certificate a server presents, inclu
passages.text:
Which command shows the certificate a server presents, including its expiry date?
s_client performs the handshake and prints the chain; -servername sends SNI so a server with several sites returns the right certificate, and x509 -dates prints notBefore and notAfter. ssh-keyscan fetches SSH host keys, and nc -z only tests the port.
man 1 openssl-s_client; man 1 openssl-x509

passages.title: Networking: Large downloads over a VPN stall while small requests work.
passages.text:
Large downloads over a VPN stall while small requests work. What is the classic cause?
Tunnels add headers, lowering the MTU. Path MTU discovery depends on ICMP; when a firewall drops it, full-size packets are lost silently and connections hang after the handshake. Allow the ICMP, lower the interface MTU, or clamp the TCP MSS.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc1191; https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4459

passages.title: Networking: Which address is the IPv6 loopback?
passages.text:
Which address is the IPv6 loopback?
::1 is loopback, :: the unspecified address, fe80::/10 link-local addresses that every interface has, and ff02::1 the all-nodes multicast group on the link.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4291

passages.title: Networking: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
The canonical text form (RFC 5952) drops leading zeros in each group and replaces the longest run of zero groups with ::, once. Three colons in a row are never valid.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5952

passages.title: Networking: What does NAT on a home router or cloud gateway do to outgoi
passages.text:
What does NAT on a home router or cloud gateway do to outgoing packets from 192.168.1.20?
Source NAT (masquerading) lets private addresses share one public address; conntrack remembers each flow so replies are translated back. Port forwarding is destination NAT for inbound connections, and nothing about NAT encrypts.
https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3022; man 8 nft

passages.title: Networking: Which commands show whether something is listening on TCP po
passages.text:
Which commands show whether something is listening on TCP port 5432 on this host?
ss filters sockets by source port and shows listeners with -l; lsof lists the process holding the socket. ping's -p sets a payload pattern, and routes have no ports.
man 8 ss; man 8 lsof

passages.title: Networking: A client resolves a name correctly but connects to the wrong
passages.text:
A client resolves a name correctly but connects to the wrong server. `getent hosts name` shows an unexpected address. Where should you look first?
With the usual "hosts: files dns" order in nsswitch.conf, an /etc/hosts entry wins over DNS for every program, and it is easy to leave one behind after a migration. /etc/services maps port names, and ARP resolves on-link MAC addresses.
man 5 hosts; man 5 nsswitch.conf

passages.title: Ollama: On which address and port does `ollama serve` listen by defa
passages.text:
On which address and port does `ollama serve` listen by default?
Ollama binds loopback port 11434 unless OLLAMA_HOST says otherwise. The same variable tells the ollama client where to connect.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/faq.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: What does the `ollama` command do when you run `ollama list`
passages.text:
What does the `ollama` command do when you run `ollama list`?
The CLI is a client of the API at OLLAMA_HOST. With the server stopped it reports that it cannot connect; with the server up it shows what the server sees, whoever runs the command.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/faq.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: Where does a systemd-run Ollama store models, and what decid
passages.text:
Where does a systemd-run Ollama store models, and what decides it?
The server writes blobs and manifests under OLLAMA_MODELS, or ~/.ollama/models of the account it runs as. Because pulls go through the server, the client's user does not matter — a common reason models "disappear" is a server started as a different user or with a different OLLAMA_MODELS.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/faq.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: A setting in ollama.service does not take effect. Which comm
passages.text:
A setting in ollama.service does not take effect. Which command shows every file that changes the unit, drop-ins included?
systemctl cat prints the unit and each drop-in from ollama.service.d/ with its path. Drop-ins apply after the unit, so a later Environment= for the same variable wins. After editing, daemon-reload before restart.
man 1 systemctl; man 5 systemd.unit

passages.title: Ollama: Which kind of authentication does the Ollama API require fro
passages.text:
Which kind of authentication does the Ollama API require from clients?
Anyone who reaches the port can list, run, pull and delete models. Keep it on loopback and put a proxy with authentication in front for other users. The key pair in ~/.ollama identifies the installation to ollama.com.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/faq.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: A browser page at https://chat.internal.example calls Ollama
passages.text:
A browser page at https://chat.internal.example calls Ollama and gets 403; curl gets 200. What must change on the server, at the narrowest?
Ollama refuses browser requests whose Origin header is not one of its local origins or listed in OLLAMA_ORIGINS; curl sends no Origin. Listing the one page's origin fixes it; * lets every site's pages call the server from users' browsers. Binding all addresses changes who can connect, not origins.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/faq.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: In the model name `qwen2.5:0.5b`, what is `0.5b`?
passages.text:
In the model name `qwen2.5:0.5b`, what is `0.5b`?
Names are model:tag, and a missing tag means latest. Tags usually distinguish sizes and quantizations; `ollama show` reports the details, here 494M parameters at Q4_K_M.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md

passages.title: Ollama: What does Q4_K_M in a model's details describe?
passages.text:
What does Q4_K_M in a model's details describe?
Quantization stores weights in fewer bits than the 16 used in training. qwen2.5:0.5b at Q4_K_M is a 398 MB file for 494M parameters; F16 embeddings like all-minilm keep full half precision.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/import.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: What does `ollama create support-bot -f Modelfile` store on
passages.text:
What does `ollama create support-bot -f Modelfile` store on the server?
Blobs are content-addressed and shared, so a derived model costs almost no disk. The Modelfile is read once; changing it later has no effect until the model is created again. Nothing is trained.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/modelfile.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: How do you see the parameters and system prompt the server a
passages.text:
How do you see the parameters and system prompt the server actually holds for a model?
show reads the stored model. The Modelfile on disk may have been edited since; ps lists what is loaded in memory; list shows names, sizes and dates.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md

passages.title: Ollama: What does the MESSAGE instruction in a Modelfile add?
passages.text:
What does the MESSAGE instruction in a Modelfile add?
MESSAGE user … and MESSAGE assistant … build a short history that shows the model the expected style of answers (few-shot prompting). Stop sequences are PARAMETER stop; licences are LICENSE.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/modelfile.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: A model is built with PARAMETER temperature 0.2, and a reque
passages.text:
A model is built with PARAMETER temperature 0.2, and a request sends "options": {"temperature": 1.0}. Which applies to that request?
Request options take precedence over parameters stored with the model, which take precedence over server defaults. A client can therefore undo a model's tuning on every call it makes.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md

passages.title: Ollama: What does setting PARAMETER seed to a fixed number give you?
passages.text:
What does setting PARAMETER seed to a fixed number give you?
Sampling is pseudo-random; a fixed seed makes it replay the same choices given identical inputs and settings. It is a testing tool, not a quality or security setting.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/modelfile.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: What does num_ctx limit?
passages.text:
What does num_ctx limit?
The context window covers everything the model reads and writes in one request. num_predict limits the answer alone. Ollama's default window is 4096 tokens (OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH changes it).
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/faq.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: A 1,388-token prompt goes to a model with num_ctx 256. The r
passages.text:
A 1,388-token prompt goes to a model with num_ctx 256. The response has prompt_eval_count 130 and the answer looks normal. What happened?
Ollama 0.34 logs "truncating input prompt limit=130 prompt=1388 keep=4 new=130": a prompt that does not fit is cut to about half the window, keeping a few tokens from the start and the most recent text. No error is returned; prompt_eval_count is the evidence. Measured in Norboten's ollama-02 lab.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md

passages.title: Ollama: Why does a chat client resend the whole conversation with ev
passages.text:
Why does a chat client resend the whole conversation with every message?
/api/chat is stateless: the messages array is the memory. That is why long conversations get slower and eventually overflow the context window, and why clients trim or summarise old turns.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md

passages.title: Ollama: How do you ask Ollama for an answer that matches a JSON sche
passages.text:
How do you ask Ollama for an answer that matches a JSON schema?
format accepts "json" or a JSON schema, and generation is constrained to match. The documentation advises also instructing the model to answer in JSON. Temperature changes randomness, not structure.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md

passages.title: Ollama: What does num_predict limit?
passages.text:
What does num_predict limit?
num_predict caps the answer's length (-1 means until the model stops). Parallel requests are OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL; the prompt is bounded by num_ctx; loaded models by OLLAMA_MAX_LOADED_MODELS.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/modelfile.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: Which two settings multiply the size of the key-value cache
passages.text:
Which two settings multiply the size of the key-value cache Ollama reserves when it loads a model?
The cache holds per-token state for every token of every parallel slot. On a 3 GB VM qwen2.5:0.5b loaded at 4,096 × 2 with a 734 MiB peak, and at 32,768 × 8 tried to allocate 3,072 MB for the cache alone.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/faq.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: What does this print — the tokens of cache Ollama reserves f
passages.text:
What does this print — the tokens of cache Ollama reserves for OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=32768 and OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=8?
Each parallel slot gets a full context. The runtime logs the same figure when it loads (n_ctx = 262144, n_ctx_seq = 32768), which is why the cache for a small model reached three gigabytes.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/faq.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: A request to Ollama gets no HTTP response at all, `systemctl
passages.text:
A request to Ollama gets no HTTP response at all, `systemctl show ollama -p NRestarts` went up, and the journal says "Failed with result 'oom-kill'". What is the cause?
An OOM kill ends the process mid-request (the client sees the connection close) and systemd restarts the unit. An allocation failure is reported by Ollama itself as HTTP 500, with the server still running; a full queue returns 503.
man 5 systemd.resource-control; https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/faq.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: Ollama logs that a load is "projected to use 3645 MiB of hos
passages.text:
Ollama logs that a load is "projected to use 3645 MiB of host memory vs. 2973 MiB of total host memory". What does that estimate not take into account?
In Ollama 0.34 the estimate compares with the machine's memory. A unit capped at 400 MB passes that comparison and is OOM-killed as soon as it grows past its cap, as the ollama-03 lab shows.
man 5 systemd.resource-control (MemoryMax=)

passages.title: Ollama: Eight people use one Ollama server. Why can OLLAMA_NUM_PARAL
passages.text:
Eight people use one Ollama server. Why can OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=2 still be right?
Requests beyond the parallel count queue (up to OLLAMA_MAX_QUEUE, 512 by default, then 503). People rarely press enter at the same instant, and on a CPU parallel slots share the same cores anyway.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/faq.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: Which endpoint lists the models currently loaded in memory,
passages.text:
Which endpoint lists the models currently loaded in memory, with their size and when they will be unloaded?
/api/ps (ollama ps) reports loaded models with size, context_length and expires_at. /api/tags lists models on disk; /api/show describes one model's definition.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md

passages.title: Ollama: By default, how long does Ollama keep a model in memory afte
passages.text:
By default, how long does Ollama keep a model in memory after a request?
The default keep-alive is 5m. OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE changes the server default; the keep_alive request field overrides it; `ollama stop <model>` unloads immediately.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/faq.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: How do you load a model into memory before the first real qu
passages.text:
How do you load a model into memory before the first real question, and keep it loaded?
An empty /api/generate or /api/chat request loads the model (done_reason "load"); keep_alive -1, or any negative value, keeps it loaded. keep_alive 0 unloads it after the response.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/faq.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: In Ollama 0.34, a model is loaded with keep_alive "2m". A la
passages.text:
In Ollama 0.34, a model is loaded with keep_alive "2m". A later request for it sends no keep_alive, and the server's OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE is unset. When will the model unload?
Measured on the lab VM: after a 2m request, a request without keep_alive set expires_at to 2 minutes later again; after a -1 request, later requests left it loaded indefinitely. A client sending keep_alive affects every later request for that loaded model, which is worth knowing when several apps share a server.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md

passages.title: Ollama: What does `ollama stop qwen2.5:0.5b` do?
passages.text:
What does `ollama stop qwen2.5:0.5b` do?
stop frees the model's memory; the next request loads it again. `ollama rm` deletes it from disk, and the service is stopped with systemctl.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/faq.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: What does POST /api/embed return for a list of texts?
passages.text:
What does POST /api/embed return for a list of texts?
An embedding model maps text to a fixed-length vector — 384 numbers for all-minilm. Retrieval compares vectors, usually by cosine similarity, to find passages related to a question even without shared words.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md

passages.title: Ollama: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
Cosine similarity is 1 for vectors pointing the same way and 0 for perpendicular ones, whatever their length. With all-minilm on the lab VM, "disk full" and "no space left on device" scored 0.621, "disk full" and "refund request" 0.228.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosine_similarity

passages.title: Ollama: In retrieval-augmented generation, when is the embedding mod
passages.text:
In retrieval-augmented generation, when is the embedding model used and when is the chat model?
Documents are split and embedded ahead of time; at question time the question is embedded, the closest chunks are retrieved, and they are placed in the chat model's context. No training is involved, and the retrieved text must fit the context window.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md

passages.title: Ollama: A RAG index was built with all-minilm. Someone switches the
passages.text:
A RAG index was built with all-minilm. Someone switches the question side to a different embedding model. What breaks?
Distances are meaningful only between vectors from the same model. A different model means re-embedding the whole corpus; a mismatch may not even error if the dimensions happen to match.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md

passages.title: Ollama: A tool written for the OpenAI API must use a local Ollama. W
passages.text:
A tool written for the OpenAI API must use a local Ollama. What is the least change?
Ollama serves OpenAI-compatible endpoints under /v1, including /v1/chat/completions with tools. The API key the client insists on can be any string; Ollama ignores it.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/openai.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: What are Ollama's durations such as load_duration and eval_d
passages.text:
What are Ollama's durations such as load_duration and eval_duration measured in?
The API returns all durations in nanoseconds: a load_duration of 603007669 is 0.6 s. eval_count divided by eval_duration (in seconds) gives tokens per second.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md

passages.title: Ollama: A response reports eval_count 8 and eval_duration 79914000.
passages.text:
A response reports eval_count 8 and eval_duration 79914000. What does this print, in tokens per second?
79,914,000 ns is 0.0799 s; 8 tokens in that time is about 100 tokens per second — qwen2.5:0.5b on two vCPUs of the lab VM, once loaded. Durations are nanoseconds.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md

passages.title: Ollama: A long generation through nginx fails after exactly 60 secon
passages.text:
A long generation through nginx fails after exactly 60 seconds with 504, but streams fine with "stream": true. Which nginx directive is involved?
proxy_read_timeout (60 s by default) is the gap allowed between two reads from the backend. A streamed answer sends a token at a time; a non-streamed one sends nothing until generation ends.
https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_proxy_module.html#proxy_read_timeout

passages.title: Ollama: Which job is a small local model like qwen2.5:0.5b well suit
passages.text:
Which job is a small local model like qwen2.5:0.5b well suited to?
A half-billion-parameter model is fast and cheap on a CPU and keeps data local, but follows complex instructions poorly and knows little. Norboten's consultant uses one to answer from retrieved passages, not from its own knowledge.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/faq.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: Does running a model with Ollama locally send prompts to oll
passages.text:
Does running a model with Ollama locally send prompts to ollama.com?
The FAQ states that local runs are not seen by Ollama; cloud-hosted models are processed by its service. Cloud features can be turned off with OLLAMA_NO_CLOUD=1. Pulling a model does contact the registry.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/faq.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: A machine must run Ollama with no internet access. What has
passages.text:
A machine must run Ollama with no internet access. What has to happen before it is disconnected?
Models are blobs and manifests under the models directory; with them present the server needs no network. Norboten's automation image pulls qwen2.5:0.5b and all-minilm at build time for exactly this reason (424 MB).
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/faq.mdx

passages.title: Ollama: Which command answers "is the model loaded, and until when?"
passages.text:
Which command answers "is the model loaded, and until when?" from a shell?
ollama ps shows loaded models, their memory and the UNTIL column from keep-alive. list is what is on disk; systemctl status is the server process; show is a model's definition.
https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/faq.mdx

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
Negative indices count from the end, so -1 is the last element. Slicing ([-1:]) would give a list.
https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/introduction.html#lists

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
setdefault inserts the default when the key is missing and returns the stored value, so append modifies the list inside the dict.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#dict.setdefault

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
Default values are evaluated once, when the function is defined, so every call without acc shares the same list. Use acc=None and create the list inside the function.
https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/controlflow.html#default-argument-values

passages.title: Python for automation: What does the `if __name__ == "__main__":` block do?
passages.text:
What does the `if __name__ == "__main__":` block do?
A module's __name__ is "__main__" only when it is the program being run. Importing sets it to the module name, so the block is skipped — handy for scripts that are also libraries.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/__main__.html

passages.title: Python for automation: Which is the standard-library way to run a command and captu
passages.text:
Which is the standard-library way to run a command and capture its output and exit status?
subprocess.run returns a CompletedProcess with returncode, stdout and stderr. os.system only returns the status and runs through a shell; shutil.run and sys.exec do not exist.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html#subprocess.run

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
Strings compare by code point, and uppercase letters come before lowercase in ASCII. For a case-insensitive order use key=str.lower (or str.casefold).
https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sorting.html

passages.title: Python for automation: What does `python3 -m venv .venv` create?
passages.text:
What does `python3 -m venv .venv` create?
A venv links to the base interpreter and has its own site-packages, so pip installs stay out of the system Python. Scripts that need it must use .venv/bin/python — not /usr/bin/python3.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
With no separator, split() splits on runs of whitespace and drops leading and trailing whitespace. split(" ") would keep the empty strings.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.split

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 exactly; the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with math.isclose, or use decimal.Decimal for money.
https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/floatingpoint.html

passages.title: Python for automation: Which HTTP methods are idempotent by definition, so a client
passages.text:
Which HTTP methods are idempotent by definition, so a client may safely retry them?
RFC 9110 defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE, PUT and DELETE as idempotent: repeating the request has the same effect as sending it once. POST and PATCH are not, so retrying them needs an idempotency key or a server-side check.
https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-9.2.2

passages.title: Python for automation: What does `with open(path) as f:` guarantee?
passages.text:
What does `with open(path) as f:` guarantee?
The file object is a context manager: __exit__ closes it however the block ends. It does not lock the file, read it, or create it (that depends on the mode).
https://docs.python.org/3/reference/compound_stmts.html#with

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
JSON objects decode to dict, arrays to list, strings to str, numbers to int or float.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#json-to-py-table

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
b = a copies the reference, not the list, and += on a list extends it in place. Both names point at the same four-element list. b = b + [4] would have built a new list and left a alone; a.copy() or list(a) makes a real copy.
https://docs.python.org/3/faq/programming.html#why-did-changing-list-y-also-change-list-x

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
Multiplying the outer list repeats a reference to the same inner list, so both rows are one object and the change shows twice. [[0] * 2 for _ in range(2)] builds independent rows.
https://docs.python.org/3/faq/programming.html#how-do-i-create-a-multidimensional-list

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
A closure looks up i when it is called, not when it is created, and by then the loop has finished with i = 2. Binding the value at creation — lambda i=i: i — gives [0, 1, 2].
https://docs.python.org/3/faq/programming.html#why-do-lambdas-defined-in-a-loop-with-different-values-all-return-the-same-result

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
With an explicit separator, split keeps empty fields between adjacent separators. Only split() with no argument splits on runs of whitespace and drops empty strings.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.split

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
strip() removes surrounding whitespace, newline included, and rsplit(":", 1) splits once from the right — which keeps an IPv6-ish or colon-containing host part intact on the left. split returns a list, not a tuple.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.rsplit

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
Python 3 rounds halves to the nearest even integer (banker's rounding), so 2.5 goes down and 3.5 goes up. It avoids a systematic upward bias when summing many rounded values.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#round

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
Since Python 3.7, dicts keep insertion order as part of the language, and iterating a dict yields its keys. Sorting needs sorted(d).
https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#dict

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
i and s both occur four times; elements with equal counts keep the order in which they were first seen, and i comes before s in the string. most_common returns a list of (element, count) pairs.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html#collections.Counter.most_common

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
A defaultdict calls its factory for a missing key, stores the result and returns it, so hosts["db"] is a new empty list — and, as a side effect, "db" is now a key. dict(hosts) was taken before that lookup, so it has only web.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.html#collections.defaultdict

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
A generator can be consumed once. The first sum reads 0, 1 and 4; the second finds it exhausted and sums nothing. Use a list when the values are needed twice.
https://docs.python.org/3/glossary.html#term-generator-iterator

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
zip stops at the shortest input and silently drops the rest. itertools.zip_longest fills the gaps, and zip(..., strict=True) (Python 3.10+) raises ValueError when lengths differ.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#zip

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
The finally block runs on the way out of the function, after the return value is computed but before the caller receives it, so its print comes first. A return inside finally would even replace the original return value.
https://docs.python.org/3/reference/compound_stmts.html#the-try-statement

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
int() ignores leading and trailing whitespace, so "8080 " converts. It raises ValueError for anything else that is not a whole number, such as "80.5" or "80a".
https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#int

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
parent is the containing directory and .name its last component; stem is the file name without its final suffix; suffix includes the dot.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html#methods-and-properties

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
Joining an absolute path discards everything before it, as os.path.join does. It is how a user-supplied "file name" escapes the intended directory; resolve the result and check it is still inside the base (is_relative_to) before using it.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html#operators

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
subprocess.run does not raise on a non-zero exit unless check=True; it returns a CompletedProcess whose returncode says what happened. Scripts that forget both carry on after a failed command.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html#subprocess.run

passages.title: Python for automation: Why is `subprocess.run(f"grep {pattern} {path}", shell=True)
passages.text:
Why is `subprocess.run(f"grep {pattern} {path}", shell=True)` dangerous when pattern comes from a user?
With shell=True the whole string goes to /bin/sh, so input like "x; rm -rf ~" becomes a second command. Pass a list — ["grep", pattern, path] — so each argument reaches the program untouched, or use shlex.quote if a shell is truly needed. Privileges are unchanged.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/subprocess.html#security-considerations

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
json.dumps maps None to null, True to true and any tuple or list to a JSON array. Loading the result back gives a list, not a tuple — JSON has no tuple type.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#py-to-json-table

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
JSON does not forbid duplicate keys, and Python's parser keeps the last value without a warning. Pass object_pairs_hook to detect duplicates when a configuration file must not have them.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#repeated-names-within-an-object

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
>6 right-aligns in six characters, 06d zero-pads an integer to six digits, and .0% multiplies by 100 and adds a percent sign with no decimals.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/string.html#format-specification-mini-language

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
group(0) is the whole match and numbered groups count opening parentheses from the left, so group(2) is the second (\w+). The r prefix keeps the backslashes for the regex engine.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html#re.Match.group

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
re.match only matches at the beginning of the string, and "port 8080" starts with a letter. re.search scans for the first match anywhere. re.fullmatch requires the whole string.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/re.html#search-vs-match

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
os.environ is a mapping, so .get returns the default for a missing variable, and os.getenv returns None when no default is given. Only os.environ["NB_MODE"] raises KeyError.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.getenv

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
Strings sort character by character, and "1" sorts before "2" and "9". Sort addresses with key=ipaddress.ip_address to get numeric order.
https://docs.python.org/3/howto/sorting.html; https://docs.python.org/3/library/ipaddress.html

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
A /22 leaves 10 host bits: 2**10 = 1024 addresses, of which 1022 are usable hosts. It spans 10.20.0.0 to 10.20.3.255, so 10.20.3.7 is inside.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/ipaddress.html#network-objects

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
list.sort() sorts in place and returns None, by convention for methods that mutate. sorted(x) returns a new sorted list and leaves x unchanged.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#list.sort

passages.title: Python for automation: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
The | operator on dicts (Python 3.9+) merges them into a new dict, and on a shared key the right-hand value wins — the usual way to lay overrides over defaults.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#dict

passages.title: Python for automation: A script calls an HTTP API with urllib or requests. Which of
passages.text:
A script calls an HTTP API with urllib or requests. Which of these keep it from hanging forever or retrying blindly?
Neither urllib.request.urlopen nor requests has a timeout by default, so a server that accepts a connection and never answers blocks the script indefinitely. Retrying a 400 or 401 cannot help, and an unbounded loop turns an outage into a flood of requests.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/urllib.request.html#urllib.request.urlopen; https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/advanced/#timeouts

passages.title: Python for automation: Why does `pip install requests` on Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 fai
passages.text:
Why does `pip install requests` on Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 fail with "externally-managed-environment"?
The distribution ships an EXTERNALLY-MANAGED marker next to its Python, and pip honours it so that it cannot overwrite packages apt installed. Install into a virtual environment (python3 -m venv), use apt's python3-requests, or use pipx for applications. sudo makes it worse, not better.
https://peps.python.org/pep-0668/

passages.title: Terraform: What does `terraform plan` do?
passages.text:
What does `terraform plan` do?
plan refreshes state, diffs it against the configuration and prints the proposed actions without changing anything. apply changes infrastructure, init downloads providers, fmt formats files.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan

passages.title: Terraform: Why keep Terraform state in a remote backend with locking?
passages.text:
Why keep Terraform state in a remote backend with locking?
A shared backend gives everyone the same state, and a lock stops concurrent operations from overwriting each other. State still contains sensitive values in plain text — protect the backend accordingly.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/state/locking

passages.title: Terraform: A resource block is deleted from the configuration. What doe
passages.text:
A resource block is deleted from the configuration. What does the next apply do?
State still tracks the resource, so Terraform plans to destroy it to match the configuration. To stop managing it without destroying it, use a removed block (or terraform state rm).
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/resources/syntax#removing-resources

passages.title: Terraform: What is an import block (or terraform import) for?
passages.text:
What is an import block (or terraform import) for?
Import records an existing object in state and associates it with a resource address. Modules come from module blocks; all .tf files in a directory are read automatically.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/import

passages.title: Terraform: Why is for_each often safer than count for a list of similar
passages.text:
Why is for_each often safer than count for a list of similar resources?
With count, instances are addressed by index; deleting the first element shifts every index and Terraform plans to replace them. for_each addresses instances by key, so only the removed key changes.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/meta-arguments/for_each

passages.title: Terraform: Which should never be committed to the repository?
passages.text:
Which should never be committed to the repository?
State can hold secrets and belongs in a remote backend; .terraform/ is a local cache of providers and modules. The dependency lock file should be committed — it pins provider versions for everyone.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/files/dependency-lock

passages.title: Terraform: What does `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` do?
passages.text:
What does `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` do?
prevent_destroy makes Terraform refuse plans that destroy the object, including replacements. create_before_destroy changes replacement order; ignore_changes ignores attribute drift. Neither affects the provider's own console.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/meta-arguments/lifecycle

passages.title: Terraform: What is a data source?
passages.text:
What is a data source?
data blocks query existing objects (an AMI, a zone, an account ID) for use in the configuration without creating or destroying them.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/data-sources

passages.title: Terraform: An output is marked `sensitive = true`. Where is its value s
passages.text:
An output is marked `sensitive = true`. Where is its value still visible in plain text?
sensitive redacts the value in CLI output, but state stores it unencrypted. Protect the backend (encryption at rest, access control) — that is where secrets actually live.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/values/outputs#sensitive-suppressing-values-in-cli-output

passages.title: Terraform: Where do you pin a provider's version?
passages.text:
Where do you pin a provider's version?
terraform { required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 5.0" } } } sets the constraint; the lock file records the exact version selected.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/providers/requirements

passages.title: Terraform: What does HashiCorp recommend about `terraform apply -target
passages.text:
What does HashiCorp recommend about `terraform apply -target=...`?
Targeting applies a partial graph and can leave configuration and state out of step. The documentation reserves it for recovering from mistakes or working around errors.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan#resource-targeting

passages.title: Terraform: What does terraform init do?
passages.text:
What does terraform init do?
init prepares the working directory and is safe to run repeatedly; it records provider checksums in .terraform.lock.hcl. Nothing is created until apply.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/init

passages.title: Terraform: What is .terraform.lock.hcl for, and should it be committed?
passages.text:
What is .terraform.lock.hcl for, and should it be committed?
The dependency lock file makes every machine and CI run use the same provider builds. terraform init -upgrade moves to newer versions within the constraints and updates it. State locking is a backend feature and has nothing to do with this file.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/files/dependency-lock

passages.title: Terraform: What does the version constraint `~> 1.52` on a provider all
passages.text:
What does the version constraint `~> 1.52` on a provider allow?
The pessimistic operator lets only the rightmost given component increase: ~> 1.52 means >= 1.52, < 2.0, while ~> 1.52.0 means >= 1.52.0, < 1.53.0.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/expressions/version-constraints

passages.title: Terraform: What does this expression evaluate to?
passages.text:
What does this expression evaluate to?
A for expression in square brackets produces a tuple (a list), one element per input. Curly braces with key => value produce an object instead. terraform console evaluates such expressions interactively.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/expressions/for

passages.title: Terraform: What does this expression evaluate to?
passages.text:
What does this expression evaluate to?
Braces with => build an object, and the if clause drops elements whose condition is false, so only db survives with 4 × 1024.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/expressions/for

passages.title: Terraform: A resource uses `count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0`. How do you re
passages.text:
A resource uses `count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0`. How do you refer to its id elsewhere?
A resource with count is a list of instances even when there is one, so it needs an index; when count is 0, [0] is an error. one(hcloud_server.web[*].id) returns the id or null.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/meta-arguments/count; https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/functions/one

passages.title: Terraform: Why does `depends_on` exist if Terraform already infers depe
passages.text:
Why does `depends_on` exist if Terraform already infers dependencies?
References between resources build the graph automatically. depends_on is for the rare case where one resource must exist first but nothing in its arguments refers to it. Overusing it makes plans more conservative and slower; other states are read with a data source or terraform_remote_state.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/meta-arguments/depends_on

passages.title: Terraform: What does `create_before_destroy = true` in a lifecycle bloc
passages.text:
What does `create_before_destroy = true` in a lifecycle block change?
The default order is destroy then create, which means downtime and fails when names must be unique. Reversing it requires that two copies can coexist, which often means generated names.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/meta-arguments/lifecycle

passages.title: Terraform: What does `ignore_changes = [tags]` in a lifecycle block do?
passages.text:
What does `ignore_changes = [tags]` in a lifecycle block do?
The attribute is still set on create, but later differences between configuration and the real object are ignored. It is used when another system legitimately manages that attribute, such as an autoscaler changing a desired count.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/meta-arguments/lifecycle#ignore_changes

passages.title: Terraform: A resource was renamed in the configuration from `hcloud_ser
passages.text:
A resource was renamed in the configuration from `hcloud_server.web` to `hcloud_server.app`. How do you avoid destroying and recreating it?
A moved block (or terraform state mv) tells Terraform the object at the old address is now at the new one, so the plan shows a move instead of destroy and create. Keeping the block in version control lets every workspace and colleague apply the same move.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/modules/develop/refactoring

passages.title: Terraform: What does `terraform state rm hcloud_server.web` do?
passages.text:
What does `terraform state rm hcloud_server.web` do?
state rm only edits state. If the block is still in the configuration, the next plan wants to create a second server. The declarative equivalent is a removed block with destroy = false. Forcing replacement is terraform apply -replace=ADDRESS.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/state/rm

passages.title: Terraform: What does `terraform apply -replace=hcloud_server.web` do?
passages.text:
What does `terraform apply -replace=hcloud_server.web` do?
-replace forces replacement of one object in the plan, which is useful for a VM whose cloud-init should run again or that is known to be broken. It replaced the older terraform taint command.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan#replace-address

passages.title: Terraform: What does `terraform plan -refresh-only` show?
passages.text:
What does `terraform plan -refresh-only` show?
A refresh-only plan reads every object and reports drift; applying it updates state to match reality. A normal plan would instead propose changes to bring reality back to the configuration. -refresh=false is the flag that skips reading providers.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan#planning-modes

passages.title: Terraform: How should a module receive a value from the code that calls
passages.text:
How should a module receive a value from the code that calls it?
A module is a black box: variables go in, outputs come out. It cannot see the caller's locals or resources, which is what keeps it reusable. Passing whole resources as objects is fine, but still through variables.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/modules/develop

passages.title: Terraform: What does a `validation` block inside a variable do?
passages.text:
What does a `validation` block inside a variable do?
For example condition = contains(["cx22", "cx32"], var.server_type) stops a typo before any API call. Types are declared with type = and checked separately; preconditions and postconditions on resources cover relationships between values.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/values/variables#custom-validation-rules

passages.title: Terraform: Which variable definition wins when a value is given in terr
passages.text:
Which variable definition wins when a value is given in terraform.tfvars, in TF_VAR_region and with -var on the command line?
Later sources override earlier ones: environment variables, then terraform.tfvars, then *.auto.tfvars, then -var and -var-file in the order given. The default applies only when nothing sets the variable.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/values/variables#variable-definition-precedence

passages.title: Terraform: Why are a variable marked `sensitive = true` and a secret st
passages.text:
Why are a variable marked `sensitive = true` and a secret stored in state not the same protection?
Terraform writes the attributes providers return, including passwords, into state, so state must be protected: an encrypted backend with tight access. Ephemeral values and write-only arguments in recent Terraform versions keep some secrets out of state altogether.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/state/sensitive-data

passages.title: Terraform: What do `terraform fmt -check` and `terraform validate` each
passages.text:
What do `terraform fmt -check` and `terraform validate` each catch?
Both are offline and cheap, which makes them the first CI step. validate needs init for provider schemas, but it does not read state or call APIs, so it cannot know whether a server type exists.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/validate; https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/fmt

passages.title: Terraform: What does `terraform output -raw server_ip` print?
passages.text:
What does `terraform output -raw server_ip` print?
-raw prints a string, number or bool as plain text — IP=$(terraform output -raw server_ip). -json prints all outputs, or one, as JSON, which is the form for lists and maps. Outputs are read from state, so no refresh happens.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/output

passages.title: Terraform: Two engineers run terraform apply at the same moment against
passages.text:
Two engineers run terraform apply at the same moment against a backend without locking. What can happen?
Without a lock, the last writer wins and resources created by the other run become orphans that Terraform no longer tracks. Backends with locking make the second run fail fast with a lock error; force-unlock exists for a lock left by a crashed run.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/state/locking

passages.title: Terraform: What does `terraform workspace new staging` create?
passages.text:
What does `terraform workspace new staging` create?
CLI workspaces switch between states; terraform.workspace can vary names or sizes. They share the same code and backend credentials, so HashiCorp recommends separate root modules or directories when environments need different access or real isolation.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/workspaces

passages.title: Terraform: What does `terraform console` let you do?
passages.text:
What does `terraform console` let you do?
It is the quickest way to check a for expression, a cidrsubnet call or what a resource attribute holds, without writing an output and applying.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/console

passages.title: Terraform: What does `cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 2)` return?
passages.text:
What does `cidrsubnet("10.0.0.0/16", 8, 2)` return?
The second argument adds 8 bits to the prefix (/16 to /24) and the third picks subnet number 2 among the 256 that creates. It is how a VPC's subnets are derived from one range without hand-written addresses.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/functions/cidrsubnet

passages.title: Terraform: What is the purpose of a `locals` block?
passages.text:
What is the purpose of a `locals` block?
local.common_labels computed from variables avoids repeating the same map in every resource. Locals cannot be set from outside — that is what variables are — and running commands locally is a local-exec provisioner or the external data source.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/values/locals

passages.title: Terraform: Why does HashiCorp call provisioners such as remote-exec a l
passages.text:
Why does HashiCorp call provisioners such as remote-exec a last resort?
A script run at creation is invisible to plan, runs once, and a failure taints the resource. cloud-init user data, a pre-built image or a configuration tool such as Ansible keeps that work declarative or at least repeatable.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/resources/provisioners/syntax

passages.title: Terraform: A plan shows `-/+ resource "hcloud_server" "web"` with `# fo
passages.text:
A plan shows `-/+ resource "hcloud_server" "web"` with `# forces replacement` next to `image`. What will apply do?
The provider marks some arguments as immutable, and changing one requires replacement: -/+ is destroy then create, +/- is create then destroy (create_before_destroy). Data on the server's disk goes with it, which is why plans deserve reading.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan

passages.title: Terraform: Which belong in a CI pipeline that applies Terraform on merg
passages.text:
Which belong in a CI pipeline that applies Terraform on merge?
Applying a saved plan guarantees that what was reviewed is what runs, and cheap offline checks fail early. Applying from every branch races and bypasses review, and state belongs in a locked remote backend, not in Git.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/tutorials/automation/automate-terraform

passages.title: Terraform: What does a `data "hcloud_image" "ubuntu"` block do?
passages.text:
What does a `data "hcloud_image" "ubuntu"` block do?
Data sources read; resources create, update and delete. Destroying the configuration never touches objects that were only read.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/data-sources

passages.title: Terraform: A `for_each` over a map of servers uses keys "web" and "db".
passages.text:
A `for_each` over a map of servers uses keys "web" and "db". "web" is removed from the map. What does the plan do?
Instances are addressed by key — hcloud_server.this["db"] — so removing one key affects only that instance. With count, removing an element in the middle shifts every later index and replaces those resources.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/meta-arguments/for_each

passages.title: Terraform: Where should provider credentials, such as an API token, com
passages.text:
Where should provider credentials, such as an API token, come from in a shared repository?
Most providers read a documented variable such as HCLOUD_TOKEN, so the token never appears in code. A variable marked sensitive keeps it out of plan output, and .tfvars files holding secrets belong in .gitignore.
https://registry.terraform.io/providers/hetznercloud/hcloud/latest/docs

passages.title: Theory: playbooks that converge: A task is `ansible.builtin.shell: echo "x=1" >> /etc/app.con
passages.text:
A task is `ansible.builtin.shell: echo "x=1" >> /etc/app.conf`. What happens on the third run?
