Text mode uses locale.getpreferredencoding(False) unless UTF-8 mode is on, so the result depends on the machine and on how the program was started, not on the file. sys.getdefaultencoding() is about str/bytes conversions inside Python and is always utf-8; a CSV file declares nothing.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#open

passages.title: Theory: text, bytes and encodings in Python: A nightly job must read exports written in different encodin
passages.text:
A nightly job must read exports written in different encodings and write one UTF-8 summary that is not destroyed when a run fails. Which of these are needed? Select all that apply.
The inputs need their own encodings, the output needs one stated explicitly so it does not follow the machine's locale, and the atomic replace keeps the last good summary when a run fails. errors="replace" would let the job finish with U+FFFD in place of real characters, which is data loss, not robustness.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace

passages.title: Theory: output buffering and stopping cleanly: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
capture_output gives the child a pipe, so stdout is not a terminal and Python block-buffers it: isatty() is False and line_buffering is False. The text still arrives here because the child exits and flushes; a long-running service would hold it until the buffer filled. The three values are printed on the two captured lines, joined by a space here.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.stdout

passages.title: Theory: output buffering and stopping cleanly: A Python program with no signal handlers is running `time.sl
passages.text:
A Python program with no signal handlers is running `time.sleep(30)` inside a `try: … finally: cleanup()` when it receives SIGTERM. What happens?
SIGTERM's default action terminates the process, so no finally block, atexit handler or buffer flush happens. SIGINT is the one Python turns into an exception (KeyboardInterrupt). To stop cleanly, install a SIGTERM handler that sets a flag and check it where stopping is safe.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/signal.html

passages.title: Theory: output buffering and stopping cleanly: A worker appends a ledger row for each item, then records th
passages.text:
A worker appends a ledger row for each item, then records the item in a state file it rewrites with `json.dump(done, open(state, "w"))`. It is stopped between the two. What does the next start do?
The row is on disk and the state does not name the item, so the restart ingests it again — a duplicate, which is the safer of the two failures. (A stop during the json.dump itself is worse: the file is already truncated, so the state is unreadable and everything is re-ingested. That is why the state file is written to a temporary file and moved into place with os.replace.)
https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace

passages.title: Theory: output buffering and stopping cleanly: Which of these make a long-running Python program's progress
passages.text:
Which of these make a long-running Python program's progress visible in `journalctl -fu` while it runs? Select all that apply.
flush=True, line buffering and PYTHONUNBUFFERED all send each line on its way as it is produced — two from inside the program, one from the unit. The service type says how systemd decides the unit has started; it has nothing to do with buffering.
https://docs.python.org/3/using/cmdline.html#envvar-PYTHONUNBUFFERED

passages.title: Theory: the module search path: `/opt/digest/digest.py` starts with `import calendar`, and `
passages.text:
`/opt/digest/digest.py` starts with `import calendar`, and `/opt/digest/calendar.py` exists. The program is started with `cd /tmp && python3 /opt/digest/digest.py`. Which file is imported?
For a script, sys.path[0] is the directory of the script — /opt/digest — not the working directory, so the file beside the script wins over the standard library wherever the program is started from. That is also why WorkingDirectory= in a unit changes nothing.
https://docs.python.org/3/tutorial/modules.html#the-module-search-path

passages.title: Theory: the module search path: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
The child runs with / as its working directory, but sys.path[0] is the script's own directory, where calendar.py is — so the import finds that file, which has no monthrange, and hasattr is False. Renaming the helper, or running with -P / PYTHONSAFEPATH=1, gives True.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.path

passages.title: Theory: the module search path: Which of these modules cannot be shadowed by a file of the s
passages.text:
Which of these modules cannot be shadowed by a file of the same name beside your script?
sys is compiled into the interpreter (sys.builtin_module_names), so importing it never touches sys.path. json, logging and calendar are ordinary Python files in the standard library and are found on the path, after the script's own directory.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.builtin_module_names

passages.title: Theory: the module search path: A helper beside a program is called `queue.py` and breaks an
passages.text:
A helper beside a program is called `queue.py` and breaks an installed library that imports `queue`. Which changes actually fix it? Select all that apply.
Only the name matters: a different name, or a qualified one inside a package, removes the collision for every importer in the process. The working directory is not what puts the script's directory on the path, and the bytecode cache follows its source file, so neither changes the import.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/sys.html#sys.stdlib_module_names

passages.title: Theory: locks and atomic replacement: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
The parent holds an exclusive flock on the file and keeps the descriptor open, so the child's non-blocking request fails at once with EWOULDBLOCK (errno 11 on Linux). Without LOCK_NB the child would have waited instead; if the parent had closed its descriptor, the lock would have been released and the child would have acquired it.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/fcntl.html#fcntl.flock; man 2 flock

passages.title: Theory: locks and atomic replacement: A job takes its lock like this: `with open(LOCK, "w") as f:
passages.text:
A job takes its lock like this: `with open(LOCK, "w") as f: fcntl.flock(f, fcntl.LOCK_EX | fcntl.LOCK_NB)`, and then does its work. What is wrong?
An flock lock belongs to the open file description and is released when the last descriptor for it is closed — which the with block does immediately. The descriptor has to stay open for as long as the lock is needed, usually for the life of the process. LOCK_NB only means "do not wait"; all flock locks are advisory.
man 2 flock

passages.title: Theory: locks and atomic replacement: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
The new content is built in a separate file in the same directory, so the target keeps its old content until os.replace swaps the directory entry in one step. A reader therefore sees the old file or the new one and never a partial write — which is what writing into the live file would have given.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace

passages.title: Theory: locks and atomic replacement: Which statements about a systemd timer that fires while its
passages.text:
Which statements about a systemd timer that fires while its own oneshot service is still running are true? Select all that apply.
A unit that is already activating is not started twice; the timer's start waits behind the running one. OnUnitActiveSec= counts from when the previous run started, not from its end, so a run longer than the interval is followed at once by the next — measured with systemd 259, a 25-second job on a 10-second timer ran back to back. None of that constrains a run someone starts by hand or from another tool, which is why the script needs its own lock.
man 5 systemd.timer; man 5 systemd.unit

passages.title: Theory: credentials in logs, files and services: What does this print?
passages.text:
What does this print?
str(HTTPError) is "HTTP Error 403: Forbidden" — no URL — but the exception keeps the full URL in .url (and .filename), so any log line that prints the URL, or code that formats the request, publishes the token. Logging e.code rather than the exception or the URL keeps it out.
https://docs.python.org/3/library/urllib.error.html

passages.title: Theory: credentials in logs, files and services: A client authenticates with a bearer token. Which of these p
passages.text:
A client authenticates with a bearer token. Which of these put the token somewhere other people can read it? Select all that apply.
A URL with the token is written to the client's log, to proxy logs and to the server's access log; a debug line with the headers publishes it to whoever reads the journal. An environment variable is visible to the same user's processes but not written anywhere by default, and a status code carries nothing secret. (LoadCredential= is better still than an environment variable.)
man 5 systemd.exec

passages.title: Theory: credentials in logs, files and services: `/etc/app/token` is `-rw------- 1 appsvc appsvc` and `/etc/a
passages.text:
`/etc/app/token` is `-rw------- 1 appsvc appsvc` and `/etc/app` is `drwx------ 2 root root`. The service runs as `appsvc`. What happens when it reads the token?
Opening a file needs execute (search) permission on every directory in the path. /etc/app allows only root, so appsvc cannot reach the file whatever the file's own mode says. The directory wants 0755, or 0750 with a group the service is in.
man 7 path_resolution; man 1 chmod

passages.title: Theory: credentials in logs, files and services: Which command tells you what account a running service uses,
passages.text:
Which command tells you what account a running service uses, without reading its unit file?
systemctl show prints the unit's resolved properties, drop-ins included; an empty value for User means the service runs as root. systemctl status shows the processes and their command lines but not the configured user, and the journal says nothing about it.
man 1 systemctl

passages.title: Theory: users, groups and permissions: What does `usermod -G devops kmorris` do if kmorris is curre
passages.text:
What does `usermod -G devops kmorris` do if kmorris is currently in wheel and developers?
-G sets the complete supplementary group list. To add without removing, combine it with -a (usermod -aG devops kmorris). The primary group is -g.
man 8 usermod

passages.title: Theory: users, groups and permissions: A user was just added to a group. Why does their existing SS
passages.text:
A user was just added to a group. Why does their existing SSH session still not have access?
A process's supplementary groups are set when the session starts. Log in again (or use newgrp / sg for one shell). No reboot is needed.
man 1 newgrp; man 1 id

passages.title: Theory: users, groups and permissions: In a sudoers file, what does `%devops ALL=(root) /usr/bin/sy
passages.text:
In a sudoers file, what does `%devops ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx` grant?
A leading % names a group; ALL is the host list; (root) the target user; then the allowed command with its arguments. Given arguments must match exactly.
man 5 sudoers

passages.title: Theory: users, groups and permissions: Which umask lets group members read and edit the files you c
passages.text:
Which umask lets group members read and edit the files you create?
002 removes only write for others: new files are 664, directories 775. 022 and 027 remove the group's write bit; 077 removes all access for group and others.
man 2 umask

passages.title: Theory: systemd units and targets: Unit A has `After=B.service` and nothing else about B. What
passages.text:
Unit A has `After=B.service` and nothing else about B. What happens when A starts at boot?
After= is ordering only. Pulling B in needs Wants= (or Requires= to fail with it). Ordering and requirement are independent in systemd.
man 5 systemd.unit

passages.title: Theory: systemd units and targets: What does `systemctl mask foo.service` do?
passages.text:
What does `systemctl mask foo.service` do?
A mask is a symlink to /dev/null in /etc/systemd/system; any start, including as a dependency, fails. disable only removes the install symlinks. unmask reverses a mask.
man 1 systemctl

passages.title: Theory: systemd units and targets: Which command shows a unit's effective definition, including
passages.text:
Which command shows a unit's effective definition, including every drop-in?
systemctl cat prints the unit file and each drop-in with its path, in the order systemd applies them. The vendor file alone misses overrides.
man 1 systemctl

passages.title: Theory: systemd units and targets: Which command makes the system boot to multi-user.target fro
passages.text:
Which command makes the system boot to multi-user.target from now on?
set-default changes the default.target link used at boot. isolate switches the running system now, without changing what the next boot does.
man 1 systemctl

passages.title: Theory: LVM, fstab and swap: The volume group has no free extents. Which sequence grows t
passages.text:
The volume group has no free extents. Which sequence grows the LV onto a new disk /dev/vdc?
The disk becomes a PV, joins the VG, and the LV takes the new extents; -r grows the filesystem in the same step. Creating a VG with an existing name fails; formatting the disk mounts a separate filesystem on top of the old one.
man 8 lvextend; man 8 vgextend

passages.title: Theory: LVM, fstab and swap: Why mount by UUID rather than /dev/vdb1 in /etc/fstab?
passages.text:
Why mount by UUID rather than /dev/vdb1 in /etc/fstab?
Disk order depends on detection order and hardware changes; a filesystem's UUID travels with it. blkid shows it. LABEL= works for the same reason.
man 5 fstab; man 8 blkid

passages.title: Theory: LVM, fstab and swap: Which fstab line enables an existing swap file at boot?
passages.text:
Which fstab line enables an existing swap file at boot?
Swap has no mount point (none or swap), type swap, and fsck pass 0. swapon -a activates what fstab lists without a reboot.
man 5 fstab; man 8 swapon

passages.title: Theory: LVM, fstab and swap: The machine stops at "Give root password for maintenance". W
passages.text:
The machine stops at "Give root password for maintenance". What should you look at first?
Emergency mode means something required for booting did not happen; a broken fstab entry is the classic cause. The journal names the device it waited for. Do not rely on systemctl --failed: when the device job times out, the mount is never attempted and nothing is listed as failed.
man 7 systemd.special (emergency.target); man 1 journalctl

passages.title: Theory: SELinux, firewalld and networking: Why is `chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /srv/site` not a lastin
passages.text:
Why is `chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /srv/site` not a lasting fix?
The label survives a reboot, but the policy still maps /srv/site to another type, so the next restorecon or full relabel undoes it. semanage fcontext -a changes the rule; restorecon then applies it.
man 8 semanage-fcontext; man 8 restorecon

passages.title: Theory: SELinux, firewalld and networking: nginx cannot bind port 8090 and SELinux logs a denial. What
passages.text:
nginx cannot bind port 8090 and SELinux logs a denial. What is the fix that keeps SELinux enforcing?
The policy lets httpd_t bind ports labelled http_port_t; labelling 8090 extends that. The firewall controls traffic, not binding, and ports are not files.
man 8 semanage-port

passages.title: Theory: SELinux, firewalld and networking: What does the -P in `setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect
passages.text:
What does the -P in `setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on` do?
Without -P the boolean changes in the running policy only and resets at boot. With -P it is written to the policy store as well.
man 8 setsebool

passages.title: Theory: SELinux, firewalld and networking: Where does a persistent static hostname live?
passages.text:
Where does a persistent static hostname live?
hostnamectl writes /etc/hostname, which is read at boot. The hostname command and /proc/sys/kernel/hostname change the running kernel only; /etc/hosts maps names to addresses.
man 1 hostnamectl; man 5 hostname

passages.title: Theory: recovery and the exam's traps: After resetting the root password from rd.break, why touch /
passages.text:
After resetting the root password from rd.break, why touch /.autorelabel before rebooting?
In the initramfs no policy is loaded, so passwd creates /etc/shadow unlabelled. The marker makes the next boot relabel the filesystem (restorecon on the file does the same once SELinux is loaded).
man 8 restorecon; man 8 fixfiles

passages.title: Theory: recovery and the exam's traps: Which repo file line points dnf at a local directory mirror?
passages.text:
Which repo file line points dnf at a local directory mirror?
baseurl takes a URL, and a local path is written as a file:// URL. mirrorlist expects a URL to a list of mirrors; there is no path= option.
man 5 dnf.conf

passages.title: Theory: recovery and the exam's traps: A timer unit contains `OnCalender=*:0/15`. What happens?
passages.text:
A timer unit contains `OnCalender=*:0/15`. What happens?
The unknown key is logged and skipped, which leaves the timer with no schedule at all, and systemd refuses a timer like that: "Timer unit lacks value setting. Refusing." The unit is bad-setting and cannot be started. systemd-analyze verify prints both lines before anything is enabled.
man 5 systemd.timer; man 1 systemd-analyze

passages.title: Theory: recovery and the exam's traps: Which command makes maria change her password at least every
passages.text:
Which command makes maria change her password at least every 90 days?
-M is the maximum age; -m is the minimum days between changes; usermod -e sets an account expiry date. (passwd -x also sets the maximum on some systems, but chage is the standard tool.)
man 1 chage

passages.title: Theory: addresses, moves and state: A resource block is renamed from `hcloud_volume.logs` to `hc
passages.text:
A resource block is renamed from `hcloud_volume.logs` to `hcloud_volume.access_logs` with no other change. What does the next plan propose?
Terraform tracks objects by address. The old address is in state but not in configuration, the new one is in configuration but not in state. A moved block, or terraform state mv, tells Terraform they are the same object.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/modules/develop/refactoring

passages.title: Theory: addresses, moves and state: What does `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` exit with when
passages.text:
What does `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` exit with when the plan has changes to make?
0 means no changes, 1 means an error, and 2 means a successful plan with changes. Without the flag, a successful plan exits 0 whether or not it has changes.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/cli/commands/plan#detailed-exitcode

passages.title: Theory: addresses, moves and state: A `random_password` is declared with its value marked sensit
passages.text:
A `random_password` is declared with its value marked sensitive. Where can its generated value still be read in plain text?
Sensitive only redacts plan and output display. State records every attribute, and terraform.tfstate.backup keeps the previous state, so both must be protected like the secret.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/state/sensitive-data

passages.title: Theory: addresses, moves and state: Why is a `moved` block usually better than running `terrafor
passages.text:
Why is a `moved` block usually better than running `terraform state mv` for a rename that is merged into a shared repository?
state mv edits one state, once, by hand, and nobody else's state learns about it. A moved block is part of the configuration, so each workspace and colleague gets the move on their next plan and apply. Neither changes the real object.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/moved

passages.title: Theory: count, for_each and moves: A resource uses `count = length(var.names)` with `names = ["
passages.text:
A resource uses `count = length(var.names)` with `names = ["a", "b", "c"]`. `"a"` is removed. Which instances does the next plan change or destroy?
count instances are identified by index. Removing the first element shifts every later element down by one, so each remaining index describes a different item, and the last index is out of range.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/meta-arguments/count#when-to-use-for_each-instead-of-count

passages.title: Theory: count, for_each and moves: What are the addresses of the instances of `resource "local_
passages.text:
What are the addresses of the instances of `resource "local_file" "vhost" { for_each = { shop = 8100, docs = 8102 } … }`?
for_each over a map addresses instances by key, written in quotes inside brackets. The values are available as each.value but play no part in the address.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/meta-arguments/for_each

passages.title: Theory: count, for_each and moves: A resource changes from `count` to `for_each` and the plan s
passages.text:
A resource changes from `count` to `for_each` and the plan says `x.y[1] will be destroyed (because resource does not use count)`. What does that mean?
After the switch every instance address is key-based. Old index addresses are kept only if a moved block claims them; any that remain unclaimed are planned for destruction, which is the intended outcome only for the instance you are retiring.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/modules/develop/refactoring#enabling-count-or-for_each-for-a-resource

passages.title: Theory: count, for_each and moves: When is `count` the better choice than `for_each`?
passages.text:
When is `count` the better choice than `for_each`?
count suits a number of equivalent instances, where it does not matter which one is removed, and the common count = var.enabled ? 1 : 0 pattern. Named, distinct instances belong in for_each. for_each keys must be known at plan time, and count is not deprecated.
https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/meta-arguments/count
